title: Messing Around With the Warburg Effect
body_text: Oncology researchers have been trying to exploit the Warburg effect for cancer treatment for decades now. This is a modified metabolic style that shows up in many types of cancer cells, and it’s been known since Otto Warburg’s experiments back in the 1920s (!) Put in broad terms, what you see is tumors downregulating the “usual” energy-generating systems of normal cells, i.e. oxidative phosphorylation and the citric acid cycle. Instead, they lean more on the lactic acid fermentation pathways. You usually see that kicking in under low-oxygen conditions in cells, but tumor cells use this “aerobic glycolysis” system all the time. At first glance, this seems a bit odd, because that’s markedly less efficient at generating ATP from glucose compared to the usual methods. There are several noticeable consequences, one of which is increased uptake of glucose by cancer cells (which indeed is the basis for using labeled glucose as a tumor detection method in a PET scan).Warburg himself thought that cancer cells might well have defective mitochondria and had to fall back on fermentation, and that this switchover could be the root cause of cancer in general. That wasn’t a bad hypothesis at the time, but (as usual) things have turned out to be more complicated. The Warburg effect is certainly real, but it seems to be more a result of the cancerous state than a cause of it. The reasons for this may become more clear when you look at things in terms of nutrients and not so much in terms of oxygen level. The more efficient oxidative phosphorylation is especially helpful under low-nutrient starvation conditions because it gets the most ATP out of a given amount of starting materials. When nutrients are abundant and ATP production isn’t a bottleneck, glycolysis is actually a more efficient way of delivering building blocks into the cellular pathways, not least because you don’t throw out carbon-carbon bonds by turning things into waste carbon dioxide. There’s also a hypothesis that cancer cells favor the lactate-producing pathway as a way of dealing with excess electron flux (more than what can be processed by the mitochondria), which would help produce more cytosolic NAD+ than the mitochondria could provide. But there are still a lot of things that we don’t understand about this area, despite decades of work. This new paper has some interesting material to add. They’re concentrating on pyruvate (there are a lot of angles to approach this from!) under Warburg effect conditions. Mitochondria are known to be pyruvate-deficient in tumor cells, which is driven from changes in several biochemical pathways. But the authors here use an ingenious method to alter pyruvate distribution. They engineer cells to express an unusual enzyme from a Pseudomonas bacterium in the mitochondrial matrix, a dehydrogenase that converts D-alanine directly into pyruvate. That’s a very rare amino acid in mammalian tissues, so you can administer it and thus activate the enzyme and the production of pyruvate. So that pops up “behind the lines” inside the mitochondria and suddenly restores something like normal pyruvate levels in there. (The authors call this the “Grubaw” system, which is Warburg spelled backwards). What happens then? Well, good old oxidative metabolism picks back up in the mitochondria, what with that pyruvate substrate suddenly becoming available again. And that slows the growth rate of things like human-patient-derived melanoma cells and in other lines as well. At the genetic level, a number of genes that are involved in the tumor cell phenotype (DNA replication and proliferation in general) start getting suppressed as well. A real surprise was the way that HeLa cells under these conditions start dumping their excess pyruvate (!) Under glucose-starved conditions, what pyruvate there is gets sent into the mitochondria (because oxidative phosphorylation, as mentioned above, is called for under those conditions). But when there’s excess pyruvate generated inside the mitochondria, it gets removed from the mitochondria and then pumped out of the cell entirely, where it shows up in the extracellular medium. The pathways involved for this transport seem to be unknown. Overall, this work confirms the benefits that tumor cells get from switching to glycolysis. So they do indeed downregulate mitochondrial activity, but it now appears that mitochondrial activity can itself downregulate tumor cell proliferation, giving these cells even more reason to damp down those pathways. The authors suggest that some of this is a recapitulation of the “host/parasite/symbiont” arrangements that took place as ancient mitochondria entered eukaryotic cells in the first place. And that’s something that I (for one) had never thought about!
